name: Hostile media effect
statement: Partisans on opposite sides of an issue read the same balanced news report and each side judges it slanted against them.
meaning: Two claims travel under one name and they are not tested the same way. The absolute version says each partisan group places the same coverage on its own hostile side of the scale midpoint. The relative version says only that the two groups differ in the predicted directions. Gunther and Schmitt call that weaker form the relative hostile media perception, and credit it to Gunther, Christen, Liebhart and Chia. Under it both sides can agree that a story favours one camp while the camp it disfavours sees more slant, and that still counts. The relative test is the easier one to pass. Gunther and Schmitt argue that the mechanism is not media hostility at all. A mass medium reaches an audience of strangers, and partisans read content as hostile when they picture what it will do to those strangers.

origin.who: Robert P. Vallone, Lee Ross and Mark R. Lepper
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their article ran in volume 49, issue 3, pages 577 to 585. They showed 144 Stanford students 36 minutes of network news on the Sabra and Chatilla massacre, cut from six segments broadcast between 15 and 24 September 1982. Sixty-eight described themselves as pro-Israeli, 27 as pro-Arab and 49 as neutral. On a nine-point scale where 5 meant fair and impartial, pro-Israelis rated the coverage 2.9 and pro-Arabs 6.7, F(1, 141) = 98.70, p < .001. Each side is past the midpoint in the direction hostile to itself, so this is the absolute form of the claim. An earlier version of this page called the article closed, said Unpaywall recorded no repository copy, and reported it through later papers instead. It is closed at the publisher, but a copy sits on an open course server at the University of Maryland, and it was read there on 21 September 2026.

evidence: Gunther and Schmitt ran the study that separates the effect from the medium. They recruited 64 anti-GM foods partisans at a natural foods co-op meeting and 87 pro-GM partisans at a biotechnology conference, plus 86 neutral controls. Each group read one text on genetically modified foods in two dressings. Half read it as a newspaper story clipped from USA Today, half as a composition-class essay by a university senior, with three typos added to the essay. On the six-item bias index the news article split the partisans: pro-GM readers saw it as tilted against GM foods at -0.32 and anti-GM readers saw it as favouring GM foods at 1.03, t(71) = 3.74, p < .001. The essay did not split them, at 0.60 and 0.23, t(74) = 1.01, not significant, and the source by group interaction was F(1, 142) = 11.7, p < .01. Controls rated the article -0.21 and the essay 0. Adding demographic covariates left the article result at F(1, 67) = 11.39, p < .01 and the essay result at F(1, 64) = 0.19. Their second measure asked the same people about influence on themselves and on a neutral reader. In the article the content read as neutral for one's own opinion at 0.03 and disagreeable for neutral others at -0.37, t(71) = 2.99, p < .001. In the essay it read as agreeable for both, at 0.74 and 0.33, t(75) = 4.02, p < .001. Christen, Kannaovakun and Gunther took the effect off campus, to the 1997 Teamsters strike against United Parcel Service. They posted questionnaires over a fortnight after a tentative settlement was announced but before the members voted on it. Of 92 managers and 100 Teamsters who consented, 84 and 51 returned them, alongside 54 students screened as neutral. All read one constructed Associated Press story dressed as a Los Angeles Times clipping. On an 11-point scale the Teamsters saw it as biased towards UPS at 1.1 and the managers saw it as biased towards the Teamsters at 1.2. The neutrals sat at -0.4 and 0.4, F(2, 184) = 27.77 and F(2, 185) = 23.95, both p < .001.

examples.text: Campaigners for and against a bypass read the same council summary. Each side says the writer gave more room to the other and buried their own evidence. Residents with no stake in it put the summary near the middle of the scale.

Supporters of both clubs read the same account of a disputed penalty. Each set says the reporter clearly favoured the other side. The paragraphs are fixed; what differs is which sentences each reader counts as the report's own view.

Parents who want the uniform rule relaxed and parents who want it kept read one school newsletter and each write in about its slant. Both may agree the piece leans one way, and each still sees more of the lean than the other side does.

replication.headline: The founding result holds, two field experiments on other issues repeat it, and two preregistered experiments on 1,636 Americans found the relative form for contested stories only.
replication.detail: Lo Iacono and Dores Cruz ran two preregistered experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk, labelling identical short news items as CNN or Fox News. In the police study, N = 817, a one-point rise on a seven-point conservatism scale raised perceived bias by 0.15 points when a story about an officer killing a civilian carried the CNN label rather than the Fox label, s.e. = 0.04, p < 0.001. The same contrast for a story about an officer saving a life gave 0.05, p = 0.129. In the COVID-19 study, N = 819, the contrast gave 0.23 points for coverage of protests against distancing rules and 0.20 points for coverage of compliance, both s.e. = 0.05, p < 0.001. Sharing intentions barely moved, which is the authors' own headline, though for the compliance story the same contrast shifted them by -0.11, p < 0.05. Hansen and Kim pooled 34 studies. Their abstract, read through OpenAlex, reports that the effect appears in diverse contexts at a moderate size. It says involvement raises the effect, that the effect survives at low involvement, and that neither media format nor study design moderates it. That abstract states no number, and the article itself was not obtained. Older work converges from other directions. Giner-Sorolla and Chaiken's abstract reports Mideast partisans judging coverage as biased against their own side and abortion partisans showing a much less consistent pattern. Gunther, Christen, Liebhart and Chia's field experiment on primate research found partisans judging news articles as biased in a disagreeable direction relative to the other side, and that perceived slant then shaped their estimates of public opinion. Their abstract credits projection as well, so the two accounts are not separated there. Reid's three experiments test a self-categorisation account rather than repeating the classic design, and none of them shows partisans a neutral news report. In his third, 119 undergraduates of 133 survived a manipulation check, and read Christopher Hitchens attacking Michael Moore and the Democrats, credited either to a Republican or to a Democrat think tank. Attributing it to a Republican raised perceived pro-Republican bias, F(1, 115) = 56.24, p < .001, partial eta squared = .33, qualified by the reader's own political position, F = 14.64, p < .001, partial eta squared = .11.

study.cite: Lo Iacono, S., & Dores Cruz, T. D. (2022). Hostile media perception affects news bias, but not news sharing intentions. Royal Society Open Science, 9(4), 211504.

limits: The pooled number everybody quotes was not obtained. Hansen and Kim's article sits behind Taylor and Francis, which answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge and HTTP 403 rather than a paywall notice. Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record no open copy, and searches of Semantic Scholar, OpenAIRE, BASE and Internet Archive Scholar on 21 September 2026 turned up none. BASE answered with a proof-of-work challenge and Internet Archive Scholar with a rate limit, so neither was a clean negative. A correlation of .30 circulates in search-engine summaries of that paper, and it is not published here, because a snippet is not a source. The conditions under which the effect fails are well mapped, and the original authors drew the first map. Vallone, Ross and Lepper report, in the founding article itself, that their own earlier pilot studies on Carter and Reagan coverage found no general tendency for partisans to perceive hostile rather than friendly bias. They put that down to subjects for whom the election had become a dead issue, and went looking for a fiercer one. Gunther and Schmitt's essay condition killed it, and Lo Iacono's positive police story killed it, so the content has to be one the sides are already fighting over. Gunther, Miller and Liebhart recruited 152 partisans on genetically modified wild rice and varied apparent circulation and source. Their abstract reports that reach moved bias judgements in the predicted direction while overall evaluations tended towards assimilation rather than contrast. Gunther and Liebhart, testing journalist against student and mass circulation against classroom, report in their abstract support for a categorisation bias and not for the other mechanisms proposed. Neither full text was obtained. Involvement is doing heavy lifting. Christen and colleagues found no reliable link between attitudes and perceived bias among their 122 students. Among the students who did identify with a side the direction ran the other way, though not significantly. Pro-Teamster students saw the article as favourable to the Teamsters at 0.67, and pro-UPS students saw it as favourable to UPS at 0.94. The measure itself is unstable. Litovsky showed 102 MTurk workers one New York Times report on a knife attack in Israel. Each rated eight specific features of the piece and five overall judgements, in an order set at random. Counting only whichever block came first, mean perceived bias was 3.13 for the specific features and 4.56 for the overall judgements, t(100) = 3.9, p < .001. That is a comparison between readers rather than within them, and Litovsky had too few partisans to test hostility, so she analysed the whole sample instead. Lo Iacono's design swaps the outlet label rather than holding one neutral source, so it measures a difference in slopes across outlets, which is the relative form of the claim. Their text gives a standard error of 0.06 for the null police result where their table gives 0.041.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating a relative result as an absolute one. Gunther and Schmitt's own table separates them item by item on one dataset. On perceived bias in the portrayal of GM foods supporters, both partisan groups saw the article slanted the same way and the anti-GM readers saw more of it, which is the relative effect. On the percentage of favourable content and on the author's own bias, the two groups landed on opposite sides of the neutral point, which is the absolute effect. A paper reporting that partisans differed has not shown that either side saw hostility. The second error is reading the neutral control as the true slant of the coverage. Vallone's neutral viewers did not sit at the midpoint. They rated the same tapes 3.8 where 5 meant fair, and they resembled the pro-Israeli partisans more than the pro-Arab ones on every measure. The authors decline to say which side was right, and note that self-labelled neutrals may lean without knowing it. The third error is folding this into the third-person effect. That effect compares perceived influence on oneself against perceived influence on others, and this one compares readings of content. Gunther and Schmitt connect them by mechanism rather than by measure, arguing that partisans see hostility once they picture a broad audience receiving the piece. The fourth error is inferring that the coverage was fair. Establishing a stimulus as neutral takes separate work, and Gunther and Schmitt did it with nine pretest judges and 86 nonpartisan readers whose mean bias rating was -0.21. The fifth error is expecting the perception to drive behaviour. Christen and colleagues found partisans' estimates of public opinion tracking their own views rather than the bias they had just reported, with personal opinion correlating .42 with perceived public support and -.41 with perceived opposition. Lo Iacono and Dores Cruz found the perception left sharing intentions on social media roughly where they were. Vallone, Ross and Lepper set their result beside Hastorf and Cantril's 1954 football study, which entry 174 covers. Naive realism, entry 165, is offered as the account of why the effect happens, and it is a framework rather than a rival finding.
